findings.reason: The protected app source introduces the exact generic helper parameter name index for an array position used by the missing-count function. That standalone binding violates the campaign's explicit naming standard. The inert candidate renames missing to missing_count_at, index to array_position, and previous to gap_left_position so each role is explicit. AST normalization proves these semantic renames are the only changes, while both protected sources remain untouched.

With missing_count_at, array_position, and gap_left_position, the candidate is concise, conventional, and interview-ready. The missing_before_end, left, right, middle, and gap_left_position names expose the monotone count, binary-search interval, probe, and containing-gap endpoint directly, and no exact generic local named index remains.

At array position i, nums[i] - nums[0] - i is exactly the number of omitted integers strictly after nums[0] and before nums[i]; strict ascending order makes this count non-decreasing. If k exceeds the count at the final position, all internal omissions are exhausted and the remaining offset extends directly beyond nums[-1]. Otherwise, binary search finds the first position whose count is at least k. Because the count at position zero is zero and k is positive, the preceding position exists and has fewer than k omissions. Advancing from its value by k minus its missing count lands exactly on the requested integer inside the containing gap, including its final missing value.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 1060, Python, and the native missingElement(nums, k) interface. Authenticated source evidence confirms one through 5*10^4 unique integers in strictly ascending order, values from 1 through 10^7, and one-based k from 1 through 10^8. Missing numbers are counted beginning strictly after the leftmost array value, proceed through internal gaps in numeric order, and continue without an upper bound after nums[-1]. The candidate solve adapter preserves that integer-return contract and the source's logarithmic-time follow-up.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2067455345 are algorithmically identical: both compute the same monotone missing-count formula, handle the same suffix condition, binary-search the same first count at least k, and apply the same offset from the preceding array value. The candidate preserves that exact data flow and differs from the app source only by the three semantic renames; the native Solution.missingElement wrapper and typing syntax remain the only protected structural adaptations.

The three hidden workloads grow alternating-value arrays from 128 through 8192 elements, a 64x span, and place k at the final internal omission so a linear gap scan traverses nearly the complete array while binary search performs logarithmically many probes. The exact candidate passed all ten visible correctness cases and all three performance tiers with relative growth exponent +0.00 and a 1.00x largest runtime ratio. An independently correct linear gap-scan control matched every correctness and benchmark output but failed only the calibrated complexity verdict with exponent +0.85 and an 82.73x largest ratio, cleanly distinguishing O(log N) search from O(N) scanning.

The Approach accurately derives the missing-count function, proves its monotonicity, separates the beyond-array suffix case, identifies the first boundary with at least k omissions, and derives the final offset from the preceding value. Its edge-case discussion covers one element, consecutive arrays, gap boundaries, and large k. The O(log N) time and O(1) auxiliary-space claims match the candidate algorithm and branch manifest.

The modular Reference preserves the source's unique ascending input, counting origin at the leftmost value, ordered internal gaps, unbounded continuation beyond the final value, all three examples and their explanations, all four constraints, the logarithmic-time follow-up, and both missing-count and binary-search hints. The authenticated statement contains no images, diagrams, or tables to reproduce.

The authenticated live Premium statement directly verified exactly three examples in source order with exact nums, k, outputs, and explanations; four constraints; strict ascending uniqueness; the logarithmic-time follow-up; and two hints. source_fidelity.json binds those facts and every composed local section to the reviewed statement hash cfbcd7928a76fa625adee54d6dd08333e893c055afc09fa1c94bd40d86f525c1.

coverage: The authenticated Premium statement contains exactly three examples. Their exact arrays, k values, outputs, and missing-number sequences appear first in source order, covering the first internal omission, accumulated gaps, and continuation beyond the array.

All ten ordinary correctness cases are visible samples or trials. They cover array-length endpoints 1 and 50000, value endpoints 1 and 10^7, k endpoints 1 and 10^8, the leftmost counting origin, an answer larger than the maximum input value, and strict ascending unique arrays.

Material behavior includes the first value after nums[0], several unequal gaps, a request ending exactly at an internal gap boundary, one and multiple suffix steps, consecutive input, a single-element array, and arithmetic handling of an extremely large suffix offset.

An independent linear oracle subtracts each explicit gap size from k and then applies the remaining suffix offset. It recomputed every authored expected value without using the protected monotone missing-count formula or binary search.

The oracle, protected app source, inert naming-only candidate, and immutable native Solution agreed on all 13 authored correctness-plus-benchmark inputs, 50180 exhaustive strictly ascending arrays through length six with k through 20, 5000 deterministic random legal arrays with k through 10^8, and explicit boundary inputs including a consecutive array at the maximum length 50000.

The maximum-length correctness case crosses the generic 100000-line trace guard for a terminating O(N) gap scan. A challenge-specific 1000000-step safety allowance permits that legal solution to complete, and an API regression proves it remains correct on every visible and hidden output before failing only the benchmark scaling verdict.

The 128-, 1024-, and 8192-element workloads remain hidden and performance-only, use size consistently as N, span 64x, alternate present and missing values, and place k at the final internal omission. A correct O(N) gap scan passed every output and failed only scaling against the O(log N) candidate.
